body:
Dhamma as a responsibility of government

Ashoka did not confine dhamma to advice about individual behaviour. He also described duties for the ruler and his officials, including public welfare, fair treatment and the communication of moral instructions.

His inscriptions present an ideal of government in which the emperor should work for the well-being of people and animals. These statements show the policies and measures he claimed to have introduced. They do not, by themselves, establish that every measure was implemented equally throughout the empire.

Medical treatment and public facilities

Major Rock Edict 2 describes provisions for medical treatment of human beings and animals. It also refers to bringing and cultivating medicinal herbs where necessary.

The same edict mentions wells and roadside trees intended to benefit travellers and animals.

Major Pillar Edict 7 refers to additional welfare works, including shade trees, mango groves, wells, rest houses and watering places. Such facilities were useful in a society where people, goods and animals travelled considerable distances over land.

These measures connect the moral idea of compassion with practical government action. For example, respect for living beings could be expressed not only by discouraging unnecessary killing but also by arranging treatment and access to water.

Restrictions on animal killing

Ashoka also associated welfare with the protection of animals. Major Rock Edict 1 describes restrictions on slaughter and sacrifice. Major Pillar Edict 5 identifies particular animals to be protected and occasions when killing was restricted.

The distinction matters: Rock Edict 2 is about medical treatment and public provisions, while Rock Edict 1 and Pillar Edict 5 address forms of animal protection.

Dhamma-mahamattas: officers for moral and social welfare

Ashoka appointed special officials called dhamma-mahamattas. According to Major Rock Edict 5, they were appointed in the 13th year after his coronation.

Their responsibilities included promoting dhamma, attending to the welfare of different religious and social groups, helping vulnerable people and considering the circumstances of prisoners.

These were officials of the imperial government, not a separate religious priesthood. Their functions were both moral and administrative.

Other officials and regular tours

Major Rock Edict 3 instructs officials known as Yuktas, Rajjukas and Pradesikas to undertake tours every 5 years for dhamma instruction and other official business.

The tours helped connect instructions issued from the centre with people in the provinces. They also illustrate how dhamma was intended to operate through the ordinary machinery of government.

How Ashoka spread his messages

Communication relied on several connected methods:

  • Inscriptions: Instructions were engraved on rocks and pillars so that messages could remain available at important locations.
  • Public reading: Officials were instructed to communicate the contents to people who could not read the inscriptions themselves.
  • Official tours: Officers visited different regions to explain dhamma and attend to administrative duties.
  • Dhamma-yatras: Ashoka promoted journeys devoted to meeting people, giving assistance and discussing dhamma rather than relying only on royal pleasure tours.
  • Messengers and external contacts: Ashoka's messages and declarations extended beyond his own dominions, including references to Sri Lanka, southern Indian polities and rulers in the Hellenistic world.

Major Rock Edict 8 describes dhamma-yatras, including Ashoka's journey to Sambodhi, associated with Bodh Gaya, after the 10th year of his coronation. These journeys involved contact with religious communities, elderly people and inhabitants of the countryside.

Keeping the emperor informed

Major Rock Edict 6 emphasises prompt attention to public business. It states that reports concerning the affairs of the people should reach the king at any time, even when he was occupied with personal activities.

This instruction reflects the ruler's declared responsibility to respond to matters affecting his subjects. It differs from the work of dhamma-mahamattas: one concerns the flow of reports and government decisions, while the other concerns special officers promoting dhamma and welfare.

Persuasion and moral instruction

In Major Pillar Edict 7, Ashoka distinguishes the effects of regulations from those of persuasion. He presents persuasion as especially important for encouraging people to practise dhamma willingly.

This explains why his policy used multiple methods. Laws and officials could restrict harmful conduct, but inscriptions, discussions and examples of good behaviour were intended to influence people's attitudes.

The main relationships to remember

Ashoka's dhamma combined individual moral duties, religious tolerance, public welfare measures and communication through inscriptions and officials. The Kalinga conquest provides an important historical setting for this policy, while the edicts provide direct evidence of the messages he wanted to convey.

Prelims focus

  • Major Rock Edict 2 records medical provision for humans and animals, wells and roadside trees.
  • Major Rock Edict 3 prescribes official tours every 5 years.
  • Major Rock Edict 5 records the appointment of dhamma-mahamattas in the 13th year after coronation.
  • Major Rock Edict 6 concerns regular reporting and prompt disposal of public business.
  • Major Rock Edict 8 concerns dhamma-yatras.
  • Trap: Dhamma-mahamattas, medical facilities and public reporting are associated with different edicts: 5, 2 and 6, respectively.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed pp. 79–81; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 2, printed pp. 32–34 and 47; S. Dhammika, The Edicts of King Asoka, Major Rock Edicts 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 8, and Major Pillar Edicts 5 and 7, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Welfare Measures and the Communication of Dhamma
